summary: Describes a mechanism, built on the Cryptographic Message Syntax and CMC, for setting up, distributing, and rekeying symmetric cryptographic keys. It also defines how users can be organized into groups so that encrypted content can be distributed to the group. This allows keys to be managed centrally and updated when membership changes.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a club with a secret handshake that must change whenever a member leaves. This describes how a club leader hands out new handshakes to the right people, and keeps groups organized.

subtitle: How a group of people can share one symmetric key, and how that key is handed out and replaced when membership changes.

tldr.problem: Encrypting a message for a large group with public keys means building per-recipient data and validating every recipient's certificate. A shared symmetric key avoids that, but someone has to create it, deliver it and replace it as members come and go.
tldr.mechanism: A Group List Agent generates shared key-encryption keys (KEKs) and sends them to members in signed CMC messages. A Group List Owner sets up the list, adds and removes members, and asks for rekeys using control attributes carried in CMS.
tldr.outcome: Any member of the group can decrypt CMS content encrypted under the shared key. The design was developed to support S/MIME Mail List Agents, and it relies on the GLA and GLOs being trustworthy.

today: RFC 5275 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Share a Symmetric Key
sections.content:
To send encrypted data to a group, an originator can use asymmetric algorithms or symmetric ones. With asymmetric algorithms the originator encrypts the content once under a content-encryption key (CEK), then builds per-recipient information using each recipient's public key certificate. For a large group that processing can take quite some time, and the certificates of all recipients must be collected and validated.

With symmetric algorithms the originator instead uses a previously distributed secret key-encryption key (KEK) to encrypt the CEK. Only one copy of the encrypted CEK is needed, because every recipient already holds the shared KEK. The cost is that the KEK must first reach every member, which is the job of this RFC.

Access control is coarse: every group member can read what the shared KEK protects. To keep a subset out, the sender should use a different KEK shared only with the smaller group, or switch to asymmetric algorithms. How the KEK is protected once a member holds it is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking a message for every friend one by one takes ages. If everyone shares one key, you lock it once. But first everybody has to get that key safely.

sections.title: The Roles: GLA, GLO and Members
sections.content:
The Group List Agent (GLA) does two jobs. The Key Management Agent (KMA) generates the shared KEKs, and the Group Management Agent (GMA) manages the Group List (GL) that the KEKs are sent to. The RFC then treats both as one thing, the GLA, and says that a corrupt GLA can always cause havoc.

A Group List Owner (GLO) builds the list and may change its properties or membership. There can be several GLOs. The GLO decides whether the list is managed or unmanaged, and is the only entity that may delete it. GLOs may or may not be members themselves.

The mechanism supports a range of lists, from very restrictive ones where a human decides membership to very open ones. The glAdministration setting has three values:

  • Unmanaged: prospective members can ask to be added or removed without GLO involvement.
  • Managed: members can ask, but the GLA redirects each request to the GLO for review.
  • Closed: the GLA only accepts add and delete requests from the GLO.

The RFC names three usage scenarios, all built around email: a sender using public keys to reach a Mail List Agent that redistributes with the shared KEK, a sender using a shared KEK to reach the MLA, and a sender using a shared KEK to reach the group directly.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a key maker and list keeper (the GLA), a club boss who decides who is in (the GLO), and the members. The boss can run an open club, a club where requests are checked, or a club only the boss can change.

sections.title: CMC Control Attributes
sections.content:
Rather than invent a new protocol, the RFC builds on Certificate Management over CMS (CMC). Each action is a control attribute placed in a CMC PKIData request or PKIResponse response, then protected with CMS. Fourteen attributes are defined, such as glUseKEK (create a list and assign a KEK), glAddMember, glDeleteMember, glRekey, glkCompromise and glKey (deliver the KEK).

Each attribute has a signing rule. For example, glUseKEK, glDelete and glRekey MUST be signed by the GLO, glAddMember and glDeleteMember MUST be signed by the GLO or the member concerned, and glKey MUST be signed by the GLA.

Conformance tables list which attributes each role must originate, receive or forward. The GLA MUST originate glProvideCert and glKey, and MUST receive glUpdateCert. Most others are optional: if a component implements an attribute, it must do so as the table indicates.

glUseKEK carries the key attributes the GLO wants. If they are omitted, the GLA controls rekeying, members may know about one another, the algorithm is AES-128, the KEK is valid for a calendar month, and two KEKs are distributed initially.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request is a short signed note with a label on it, like "add this person" or "here is the new key". The label says what to do and who is allowed to send it.

sections.title: Managing a Group List
sections.content:
Section 4 walks through each administrative exchange step by step, and notes that these procedures are not prescriptive. They cover assigning a KEK to a new list, deleting a list, adding and removing members, requesting a rekey, changing the GLO, reporting a compromised KEK, asking for a KEK refresh, querying the GLA, and updating a member's certificate.

Every exchange follows the same checks. The receiver looks at signingTime, verifies signatures, then checks names and the request itself. Failures are reported in a cMCStatusInfoExt using codes such as nameAlreadyInUse, unsupportedAlgorithm, noGLONameMatch, alreadyAMember and notAMember. On a managed list the GLA forwards member requests to the GLO with an extra SignedData layer.

When to rekey is a policy choice. Unmanaged lists should typically not be rekeyed when someone joins, as the overhead becomes prohibitive for a large group. Managed and closed lists can be rekeyed to keep traffic confidential, or a new list with a different key can be created. A closed or managed list needs a rekey when a member is removed, and rekeying an unmanaged list on deletion is not advised.
sections.plainLanguage: Each job, such as adding a friend or changing the lock, is a little back-and-forth. The helper checks who asked and whether it makes sense, then says yes or explains why not.

sections.title: Delivering and Replacing Keys
sections.content:
The GLA distributes shared KEKs with the glKey message. It carries the list name, a key identifier, the wrapped KEK in RecipientInfos, the algorithm, and glkNotBefore and glkNotAfter validity times. Times are in UTC (Zulu), include seconds and have no fractions. The ktri choice MUST be supported, and the KEK MUST be generated as the CMS random number guidance requires.

A glKey is sent after a member is added, after a compromise report, after a refresh request, after a member is deleted from a managed or closed list, and after a rekey. If the GLO set recipientsNotMutuallyAware to true, a separate glKey goes to each member, so no member learns who else is on the list.

The generationCounter says how many KEKs to issue. At least two are distributed initially, so the second can take over when the first expires. The duration field counts days of validity, and zero means a calendar month. A member that receives a valid glKey should store the KEK safely, tied to the list name and key identifier, and MUST reply with a success status.
sections.plainLanguage: New keys arrive in a signed envelope only the right members can open. The helper sends a spare key too, so the club never gets stuck when one key runs out.

sections.title: Protection, Algorithms and Security
sections.content:
At a minimum every request and response MUST be wrapped in a SignedData. An EnvelopedData may be added for confidentiality, and another SignedData over that. If a request is encrypted, the GLA MUST be a recipient. All messages MUST include signingTime, and nonces can be used for replay prevention, though only if state is kept. SMTP MUST be supported for transport.

On algorithms, a KEK being distributed MUST be protected by a key of equal or greater length, and the shared KEK algorithms are those in the CMS algorithm and AES documents.

The security section stresses several points:

  • GLOs control setup, rekeying and membership, so only trusted GLOs should be used.
  • If a member is removed from a closed or managed list without a rekey, that member keeps the group key and can keep decrypting.
  • Members that store a KEK must record which GLA sent it, so later rekeys come from the same entity.
  • Large generationCounter and long duration values give attackers time. The RFC's example is 14 keys valid for a year each, which gives an attacker at least 13 years against the last key.
  • If one KEK in a chain of KEKs is compromised, all later KEKs in the chain MUST be considered compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is signed so nobody can fake a note. If someone leaves the club, you must change the lock, or they can still get in. And keys should not last so long that burglars have years to try.

items.label: glUseKEK
items.desc: GLO asks that a shared KEK be assigned to a list.

items.label: glDelete
items.desc: GLO asks that a list be deleted.

items.label: glAddMember
items.desc: GLO or prospective member asks to add a member.

items.label: glDeleteMember
items.desc: GLO or member asks to remove a member.

items.label: glAddOwner
items.desc: Allow a new GLO to administer the list.

items.label: glRemoveOwner
items.desc: Disassociate a GLO from the list.

items.label: glkCompromise
items.desc: Report that a shared KEK is compromised.

items.label: glkRefresh
items.desc: Member asks for the KEK to be sent again.

items.label: glProvideCert
items.desc: GLA or GLO asks a member for a new encryption certificate.

items.label: glUpdateCert
items.desc: Member or GLO supplies a new certificate.
